questions.stem_markdown: During a non-urgent consent discussion in a Sydney paediatric clinic, a mother answers every question for her 16-year-old son and says the team can rely on her explanation because she is the parent. What is the **best response** based on the notes?

options.text: That is appropriate, because parental explanation replaces direct assessment of the adolescent
The clinician still needs to hear directly from the adolescent because competence depends on the young person's own maturity and understanding
Direct questions should only be asked if the parent leaves the hospital entirely
Parental agreement automatically proves that the adolescent is competent
Because the patient is 16, the parent should not be involved at all

questions.explanation_markdown: The notes describe legal competence to consent as depending on factors belonging to the **minor**, including maturity, understanding, intelligence, experience, and ability to weigh consequences. A parent can support the discussion, but cannot substitute for direct assessment of the adolescent's own understanding.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes assess competence by looking at the minor's own capacities, not by relying only on a parent's explanation.
why_others_wrong.C: The source material does not require complete parental exclusion in order to speak with the adolescent directly.
why_others_wrong.D: Parental agreement is not listed as proof of competence in the notes.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes do not say parents are never involved once a patient is 16; the issue here is that the adolescent's own understanding still needs assessment.

key_takeaways: Consent assessment focuses on the adolescent's own capacities.
Supportive parent involvement is different from letting the parent replace the adolescent's voice.
Direct discussion with the young person remains important in non-urgent consent conversations.

questions.stem_markdown: A 17-year-old has long managed routine day-to-day decisions for a chronic condition. The team is now discussing a much more serious elective intervention with major long-term consequences. Why should the clinician assess decision-making capacity especially carefully in this situation?

options.text: Because the gravity or seriousness of the proposed treatment is one of the factors relevant to competence assessment
Because any decision after age 16 no longer needs capacity assessment
Because chronic illness automatically prevents a young person from being competent
Because only the parents can decide when a treatment is serious
Because seriousness matters only in emergency treatment

questions.explanation_markdown: The notes list the **gravity or seriousness of the treatment** as one of the factors taken into account when assessing a minor's legal competence to consent. A young person who handles low-stakes choices well may still need a more careful assessment when the decision is substantially more consequential.

why_others_wrong.B: The notes do not remove the need for capacity assessment at age 16.
why_others_wrong.C: Chronic illness is not described in the notes as automatically preventing competence.
why_others_wrong.D: The seriousness of treatment is a factor for clinical assessment, not something decided only by parents.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes include seriousness of treatment as part of competence assessment generally, not only in emergencies.

key_takeaways: Capacity assessment is decision-specific rather than fixed once and for all.
Higher-stakes decisions require more careful exploration of understanding.
The seriousness of treatment is explicitly listed in the notes as relevant to consent assessment.

questions.stem_markdown: A treatment dispute between a 16-year-old, parents, and the treating team has continued despite repeated discussion and other management steps. According to the notes, how should a court order be viewed in this pathway?

options.text: As the first routine response whenever a parent and adolescent disagree
As an administrative shortcut that replaces further family discussion
As a last-resort step to authorise treatment after other measures have been tried
As something relevant only once the patient turns 18
As something used only for experimental procedures

questions.explanation_markdown: In the refusal-and-conflict section, the notes describe a **court order** as the **last-resort** mechanism to authorise treatment. This places it at the end of the pathway rather than at the beginning of every disagreement.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes do not describe court involvement as the routine first step in disagreement.
why_others_wrong.B: The source material presents court involvement as escalation, not as a replacement for discussion and other management steps.
why_others_wrong.D: The notes discuss court involvement within the context of minors, not only after adulthood.
why_others_wrong.E: The court-order point is broader than experimental procedures alone.

key_takeaways: Court involvement is presented as escalation rather than routine management.
Not every disagreement requires immediate legal action.
The notes frame court orders as a last-resort authorisation step.

questions.stem_markdown: A trainee reads the notes on **special medical treatment (<16 years old)** and tries to apply that pathway automatically to a 16-year-old with an unusual proposed intervention. What is the **best correction**?

options.text: That is correct, because every minor automatically falls under the under-16 special medical treatment pathway
That specific special medical treatment category in the notes is for those under 16, so it should not be applied automatically to a 16-year-old
That is correct, because all 16-year-olds are treated exactly as adults in the notes
That is correct, because special medical treatment is simply another term for emergency treatment
That is correct, because the parent's preference alone decides whether the under-16 pathway applies

questions.explanation_markdown: The notes label this section **Special Medical Treatment (<16 years old)** and separately distinguish a **child** as 15 or younger from a **young person** aged 16 or 17 in the NSW framing. That means the under-16 pathway should not be assumed automatically for a 16-year-old simply because they are still a minor.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes do not say that every minor falls under the under-16 special medical treatment category.
why_others_wrong.C: The notes still describe a 16-year-old as a minor, not as an adult.
why_others_wrong.D: Special medical treatment and emergency treatment are described as different concepts in the notes.
why_others_wrong.E: Parental preference does not determine whether the under-16 category applies.

key_takeaways: The notes distinguish under-16 pathways from broader minority status.
A 16-year-old is still a minor, but not automatically part of the under-16 special medical treatment category.
Applying the right consent pathway depends on the specific note-defined category.

questions.stem_markdown: A 15-year-old with gender dysphoria attends with her mother and stepfather, both of whom support proceeding with gender-affirming medical treatment. Her biological father also has parental responsibility but has not been consulted. Based on the notes, what is the **main unresolved issue**?

options.text: Whichever adult attends the appointment can provide the necessary parental consent
The adolescent's agreement alone is enough if she appears Gillick competent
Consent should come from both parents or all people with parental responsibility
The stepfather's support replaces any need to consider other parental responsibility arrangements
Parental consent is irrelevant once the patient is 15

questions.explanation_markdown: For gender-affirming medical treatment, the notes state that **parental consent is required** and specify **consent of both parents or all persons with parental responsibility**. In this scenario, that issue remains unresolved because one person with parental responsibility has not been included.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes do not say that any one attending adult is enough.
why_others_wrong.B: The source material specifically says parental consent is required for this pathway.
why_others_wrong.D: A supportive stepparent does not replace the need to consider all persons with parental responsibility as described in the notes.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes do not make parental consent irrelevant at age 15 for this treatment pathway.

key_takeaways: The notes give a distinct consent pathway for gender-affirming medical treatment.
Parental responsibility matters, not just who attends the clinic visit.
Clinicians need to clarify who actually holds parental responsibility.

questions.stem_markdown: A 15-year-old is avoiding follow-up appointments because she assumes any Medicare-linked healthcare must stay fully under parental control and therefore cannot be arranged more independently. What is the **best counselling response** based on the notes?

options.text: Independent attendance is not realistically possible until adulthood, so follow-up should wait
Medicare arrangements do not change during adolescence, so privacy concerns cannot really be addressed
Some Medicare arrangements change during adolescence in ways that can support more independent access and privacy, so the practical options are worth discussing
Medicare only affects hospital admissions, so it is unrelated to outpatient follow-up access
The only way to make follow-up more private is to move entirely outside Medicare-linked care

questions.explanation_markdown: The Medicare section of the notes describes adolescent-specific changes that can support **more independent access and privacy** in healthcare. In a young person who is avoiding follow-up because of these concerns, the best response is practical counselling that such options exist and are worth discussing.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes describe adolescent Medicare changes rather than requiring total dependence on parents until adulthood.
why_others_wrong.B: This directly contradicts the note-based point that Medicare arrangements do change during adolescence.
why_others_wrong.D: The notes present Medicare changes as relevant to adolescent healthcare access more broadly, not only to admissions.
why_others_wrong.E: The source material does not say that independence or privacy requires leaving Medicare-linked care completely.

key_takeaways: Service-access barriers can reduce adolescent follow-up.
The notes describe Medicare changes that may support more independent attendance and privacy.
Practical systems counselling can be part of adolescent care.
